title: Governance Design for a Clinical-Intake Assistant
description: Tests the ability to sequence a compliance gate before design, name specific risks rather than generic ones, map each risk to a structural control, place a human-in-the-loop gate at the correct point, and build in transparency logging from the start.

scenario.background: A regional hospital network wants to deploy a Claude-powered clinical-intake assistant: patients describe symptoms in natural language, and the system drafts a structured intake summary plus a preliminary triage-urgency flag for the attending nurse.

characters.name: Dr. Priya Ramanathan
characters.concern: A missed urgent case caused by an over-trusted or biased triage flag is a patient-safety incident, not just a quality bug.

characters.name: James Whitfield
characters.concern: No PHI may be processed by the model provider until a signed BAA is in place — this cannot be a parallel workstream.

questions.stem: Where does James's BAA requirement belong in the project timeline?
options: It can proceed in parallel with architecture design, since it doesn't block any technical work
It's a prerequisite that must be signed before any PHI processing begins, and before design work is finalized — not a parallel workstream
It only needs to be in place before the system goes live in production, not before design
It's Legal's responsibility entirely and doesn't need to be tracked by the architect
questions.explanation: B is correct because the system touches PHI, and a signed BAA with the model provider is a hard prerequisite — no BAA, no PHI processing, full stop — which means it has to be resolved before design work is finalized, not treated as a parallel or later-stage task. A and C both risk finalizing a design (or reaching production) around an assumption that later turns out to be legally unavailable. D ignores that the architect is accountable for sequencing this correctly into the project plan, even though Legal owns executing it.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a named risk to its structural control is correct for this system?
options: Bias risk → a generic reminder in the system prompt to 'be fair to all patients'
Bias risk → disaggregated evaluation of triage-flag accuracy broken out by age, sex, and other relevant subgroups before launch, not just aggregate accuracy
Data leakage risk → trusting the framework's default session behavior without verifying isolation in testing
Hallucination risk → a longer system prompt asking the model to 'be careful and accurate'
questions.explanation: B is correct because a triage-urgency model that systematically under-flags urgency for a demographic subgroup is both an ethical and patient-safety failure, and the only way to catch that pattern is disaggregated evaluation — aggregate accuracy alone can hide it. A is a soft prompt-level nudge, not a structural control, and doesn't measure anything. C explicitly assumes what should be verified — data leakage requires hard per-session isolation confirmed through testing, not an assumption. D is another soft instruction; the actual structural control for hallucination is requiring every symptom claim in the output to be traceable to the patient's actual input text.

questions.stem: Given the high consequence severity (a missed urgent case) and a well-defined action space (a nurse reviews before scheduling), where should the human-in-the-loop gate sit, and how should the interface support it?
options: Full autonomy with no human review, since the model is generally reliable
An approve-before-action gate, with the interface displaying the source symptom text alongside the flag so the nurse's fastest path is reading the evidence, not just clicking a checkmark
Lightweight post-hoc sampling of a small percentage of intake summaries per week
A human review step, but with only the final urgency flag shown, to keep the interface simple
questions.explanation: B is correct because high consequence severity plus a well-defined action space is squarely the case for an approve-before-action gate, and displaying the source text alongside the flag specifically counters automation bias — a nurse under time pressure needs the evidence visible, not just a label to rubber-stamp. A skips review entirely for a high-severity, patient-safety-relevant decision. C is a detective, after-the-fact control that can't prevent a missed urgent case before it happens. D creates exactly the automation-bias risk the interface design is meant to counter, since the nurse has nothing but the label to click through.

questions.stem: What transparency practice should be built in from the start, and why?
options: Log only the final triage-urgency flag, since that's the only output that matters
Log the source patient text, the specific reasoning that drove the urgency flag, and the nurse's confirm/override decision — so a later-challenged triage decision can be reconstructed
No logging is needed if the human-in-the-loop gate is already in place
Log only cases the nurse overrides, since agreed-with cases carry no risk
questions.explanation: B is correct because if a triage decision is later challenged — a missed urgent case, a complaint, a regulatory inquiry — the system must be able to reconstruct *why* the flag was set and what the nurse decided, not just what the final flag was. A discards the reasoning and source evidence needed to reconstruct the decision later. C conflates having a review gate with having a durable record of what happened at that gate — they're separate requirements. D wrongly assumes agreed-with cases carry no future risk; a later-discovered systematic bias could affect confirmed cases too, and without logging them there's no way to audit the pattern.

keyLearnings: A compliance gate that blocks legally-required work (like a signed BAA before PHI processing) is a prerequisite, not a parallel workstream — it must be resolved before design finalizes.
Governance risks (hallucination, bias, over-reliance, data leakage) each need a specific, structural control mapped to them — a generic prompt reminder or an unverified assumption is not a control.

The correct point for a human-in-the-loop gate is set by consequence severity and how well-defined the action space is — high severity plus a clear approval point calls for an approve-before-action gate, with an interface designed to counter automation bias.
Transparency logging must capture the reasoning behind a decision and the human's response to it, built in from the start, so a later-challenged decision can be reconstructed.
